sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Single Leg Hip Thrust is a unilateral glute exercise performed with your upper back supported on a bench and one leg extended while the other drives the movement.

This variation isolates each glute individually, making it highly effective for identifying and correcting strength imbalances between sides.

By working one leg at a time, the single leg hip thrust increases the demand on the working glute and challenges core stability throughout the movement.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Isolates each glute individually for balanced development
- Identifies and corrects strength imbalances between sides
- Increases glute activation compared to bilateral hip thrusts
- Improves single-leg stability and balance
- Builds functional unilateral hip extension strength
- Minimal equipment required
- Enhances core stability and coordination

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Glutes (Gluteus Maximus), Gluteus Medius

Secondary: Hamstrings, Quadriceps, Hip Adductors, Core, Erector Spinae

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Sit on the ground with your back against a bench, positioned at around shoulder blade height.
2. Place one foot flat on the ground with the knee bent at approximately 90 degrees.
3. Extend the other leg straight out in front of you.
4. Hold a dumbbell on your hip or keep your hands on your hips for balance.
5. Keep your chin slightly tucked and your gaze forward.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Drive through the heel of your planted foot to lift your hips off the ground.
2. Push your hips upward until your thigh is parallel to the floor.
3. Squeeze your glute hard at the top of the movement.
4. Keep the extended leg straight and elevated throughout the rep.
5. Maintain a neutral spine — avoid hyperextending your lower back.
6. Slowly lower your hips back down to the starting position with control.
7. Repeat for the desired number of reps before switching sides.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Hyperextending the lower back at the top of the movement
- Allowing the hips to rotate or tilt to one side
- Pushing through the toes instead of the heel
- Not keeping the extended leg straight and stable
- Positioning too far forward or back on the bench
- Not achieving full hip extension at the top
- Rushing through reps without controlling the descent
- Neglecting to train both sides equally

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Sturdy Flat Bench or Box
- Flat, Non-Slip Floor Surface
- Optional: Dumbbell or Kettlebell (for added resistance)
- Optional: Hip Pad or Towel (for comfort if using weight)

sections.heading: Bench Setup
sections.content:
1. Position a sturdy bench against a wall or rack so it doesn't slide.
2. The bench height should allow your shoulder blades to rest on the edge.
3. Ensure the bench is stable and won't tip during the movement.
4. If using a box, make sure it is heavy enough to stay in place.
5. A standard flat bench height works well for most people.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Working Foot: Flat on the floor, positioned so the shin is vertical at the top.
2. Non-Working Leg: Extended straight out in front, elevated off the floor.
3. Back: Shoulder blades resting on the edge of the bench.
4. Arms: Hands on hips or holding a dumbbell across the working hip.
5. Head: Neutral position, chin slightly tucked.
6. Core: Braced throughout to prevent hip rotation.
7. Hips: Level and square throughout the entire movement.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Bodyweight Hip Thrust: Bilateral version with no external load
- Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Bilateral version with dumbbell resistance
- Kettlebell Hip Thrust: Bilateral version with kettlebell resistance
- Single Leg Glute Bridge: Floor-based unilateral version
- Barbell Hip Thrust: Heavier bilateral loading option
- Bulgarian Split Squat: Unilateral lower body compound exercise

sections.heading: Single Leg Variations
sections.content:
Single Leg Hip Thrust: Standard unilateral bench-supported thrust
Weighted Single Leg Hip Thrust: Added dumbbell or kettlebell for resistance
Paused Single Leg Hip Thrust: Hold at top for increased time under tension
Single Leg Glute Bridge: Floor-based unilateral alternative
Elevated Foot Single Leg Hip Thrust: Foot raised for extra range of motion
Tempo Single Leg Hip Thrust: Slow eccentric for enhanced muscle engagement

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Balance Issues: Start with bilateral hip thrusts to build base strength
Knee Discomfort: Adjust foot position closer or further from the bench
Lower Back Pain: Focus on core bracing and avoid hyperextension
Hip Rotation: Engage your core more and reduce range of motion initially
Not Strong Enough: Begin with single leg glute bridges from the floor
Want More Resistance: Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell on the working hip
